conceptTag: Plan a year with uncertain sales
readerTitle: Plan a year when you can't predict your sales
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (B2B 디자인 에이전시와 대형 유통사 안의 마케팅팀 고객) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 불확실한 해의 계획은 숫자 하나를 맞히는 일이 아니라, 경우마다 할 일과 그 신호를 미리 정해 두고 실제 숫자를 보며 고쳐 가는 일이다.
misconception: 매출을 예측할 수 없으면 계획을 세워도 소용없다. 계획은 정확한 숫자 하나를 맞혀야 의미가 있다.

sources.text: 관리회계·재무계획의 표준 개념 (시나리오 계획, 계획 대비 실적, 롤링 포캐스트, 인력 계획)
모든 기업명과 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 시나리오: 작년 매출 $2.4M, 최대 고객 비중 30% = $720k. 이 고객이 지출을 절반으로 줄이면 $2.4M − $360k = $2.04M(카드에는 약 $2.0M). 기본 $2.5M, 높음 $3.0M. 현재 팀 비용 연 $2.2M이므로 낮은 경우 약 $200k 적자.
채용: 디자이너 2명 × 연 약 $100k = $200k 추가. 낮은 경우 비용 $2.4M vs 매출 $2.0M → 약 $400k 적자.
1분기: 계획 $2.5M ÷ 4 = $625k. 유통사 고객 분기 계획 $180k($720k ÷ 4), 실제 $95k. 나머지 고객 계획대로 $445k. 실적 $445k + $95k = $540k. 부족분 $85k, 계획 대비 13.6%(약 14%) 미달.

cards.title: Plan a year when you can't predict your sales
body: Maya runs Northline, a 14-person design agency that works for other businesses. Last year it billed $2.4M.

Nearly a third came from one client: the in-house marketing team of a large home-goods retailer. That team just told her its parent company is reviewing every budget. Maya has to plan next year anyway. You'll make her four big calls.

image.label: Agency owner looking at a calendar full of question marks
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 디자인 스튜디오 책상에 앉은 대표가 12개월 달력을 보고 있고, 달력 칸마다 물음표. 한쪽에 큰 고객사 건물 모형이 그림자처럼 드리움. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What kind of plan do you write?
body: Your current team and rent cost about $2.2M a year. The big client might renew, cut back, or grow. Two new clients are also talking to you.

options.text: One best-guess number, $2.5M, and plan around it
options.feedback: Simple to share, but it says nothing about what to do if the big client cuts back. You'd be making that call in a panic later.

options.text: Three cases, low, base and high, each with actions and the signal that triggers them
options.feedback: More work up front. In return, the hard decisions get made calmly now, not in a rush mid-year.

options.text: Wait until the client's budget review ends, then plan
options.feedback: You'd plan with better facts, but you'd spend months hiring, spending and pricing with no plan at all.

cards.title: Each case comes with a trigger and a move.
body: The low case is the one that matters most. It runs about **$200k below** what the current team costs, so Maya knows ahead of time what she'd cut.

breakdown.label: Low
breakdown.detail: Big client halves its spend. Freeze hiring, cut freelancers.

breakdown.label: Base
breakdown.detail: Current clients renew. Run the plan as written.

breakdown.label: High
breakdown.detail: Two new clients sign. Add designers.

cards.softwareNote: In a subscription software business, the low case is often a list: which accounts renew this year, and on what dates. Each renewal date is a natural trigger to check.

cards.title: The high case needs two more designers.
body: Each designer adds about $100k a year in cost. Good designers take two months to find. When do you hire?

options.text: Hire both now so you're ready for growth
options.feedback: Ready for the high case, but in the low case costs hit $2.4M against $2.0M in sales. Salaries are the hardest cost to undo.

options.text: Use freelancers now; hire one permanent designer when the first new client signs
options.feedback: Freelancers cost more per hour but can stop any month. Each hire is tied to signed work, not hope.

options.text: Hire no one this year, whatever happens
options.feedback: Safe on cost. But if both clients sign, an overloaded team misses deadlines and you may lose the new work.

cards.title: Sales came in 14% below plan.
body: Say you chose freelancers. The quarter's plan was $625k; actual sales were $540k. The whole gap is the big client: its team paused two projects while head office reviews spending. Every other client is on plan. What now?

options.feedback: Avoids overreacting, but you ignore a clear signal. If the pause becomes a cut, you've lost three months to prepare.

options.text: Switch to the low case right away: cut freelancers and all events
options.feedback: Protects cash, but you'd shrink the whole business over one client's pause and risk the healthy accounts.

options.text: Ask the client team when their budget is set, and lower the forecast for that client only
options.feedback: The gap has one cause, so the fix targets that cause. You also learn the date that decides your low case.

cards.title: The client's new budget is in.
body: Say you asked. The retailer's team got a fixed budget from head office: half its usual agency spend until year end. Meanwhile, one new client signed. Your January plan no longer matches reality. How do you plan from here?

options.text: Keep steering by the January plan
options.feedback: Easy, but every decision now rests on numbers you know are wrong.

options.text: Throw out the January plan and write a new one
options.feedback: Current numbers, but you lose the record of what you expected, so you can't learn why you missed.

options.text: Keep January as the yardstick, and each quarter forecast the next 12 months
options.feedback: You keep score honestly and steer with fresh numbers. The 12-month view also covers the client's next budget cycle.

cards.callout: Your client's budget calendar is part of your forecast. Pitch before their year is set, not after.

cards.title: Scenarios and updates have costs too.
body: Three cases only help if each has a clear trigger and action. Ten cases with no triggers is just worry in a spreadsheet.
Frequent updates can also become excuses. If the forecast always moves to match results, nobody ever misses. That's why the original plan stays as the yardstick.
And triggers work only if someone checks them on a schedule, not when it feels urgent.

image.label: Three signposts at a fork, each with a small flag
image.brief: 갈림길에 표지판 세 개 "Low", "Base", "High". 각 표지판 옆에 작은 깃발(신호)과 도구 상자(할 일)가 놓여 있음. 차분한 파스텔 톤. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Decide in advance, then update on schedule.
body: You can't predict an uncertain year. You can decide now what you'll do in each case, and check the real numbers often enough to switch in time.
**Try it today:** write your low case for next quarter in one line: what sales would be, the signal you'd see first, and the first cost you'd cut.
list: **Decision 2:** hires tied to signed work = *planning headcount*
**Decision 3:** find the cause of the gap = *plan vs actual*
**Decision 4:** fixed yardstick plus fresh outlook = *rolling forecasts*
